events.excerpt: A Zcash governance trilogy, part 3 of 3. Or navigating the dark forest without turning on all the lights TL;DR: In a private system we cannot know who holds voting power, how many people sit behind it, or whom they are connected to. The answer is not to abolish the privacy. It is to bound what any vote can decide, so that capturing one voting mechanism cannot confer control over the whole system. Part 1: An Ode to Rough Consensus . Part 2: When We Disagree: Making Rough Consensus Work . Zcash is building a parallel financial system, outside of but adjacent to the existing one. Its governance, however, remains entirely inside human institutions. That private financial system starts from a different assumption from the one we have become accustomed to elsewhere: privacy is normal. In such a system, private by default should be the ordinary situation, not a special mode for people with something to hide. Traditional finance already runs part of its markets this way. Dark pools let large investors trade without displaying their orders, so that others cannot trade against them. Dark does not mean lawless. events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. Added a test covering both cases. Test plan CI/PT Release notes Check each box that your changes affect. If none of the boxes relate to your changes, release notes aren't required. For each box you select, include information after the relevant heading that describes the impact of your changes that a user might notice and any actions they must take to implement updates. Protocol: Nodes (Validators and Full nodes): gRPC: JSON-RPC: GraphQL: CLI: Rust SDK: Indexing Framework: Co-authored-by: Claude Fable

events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. Because leanVM has no authority, a leanVM bug can’t break Ethereum’s security or halt the chain. At the same time, leanVM runs on mainnet under real load, so
events.headline: EIP Draft: Run leanVM aggregation in shadow mode alongside BLS until PQ/AI day

The Nasdaq-listed company held 94.68 bitcoin, valued at $7.9 million, as of Sept. 30. That compares with 293.14 bitcoin worth about $17.2 million at the end of June, according to its second-quarter results . That implies Rumble parted with roughly 198 bitcoin during the quarter, or about 68% of its stack. The company’s cash-flow statement shows a net sale of digital assets of about $15.3 million for the first nine months of 2026. In the same period a year earlier, it spent $19.1 million buying digital assets. Rumble did not explain the sales in its release, and it did not say what price it received. The balance sheet’s digital assets line, which the release does not break down, fell to $11.1 million from $18.5 million at the end of 2025. events.excerpt: Hello Zcash Community! I have submitted a second Q4 retroactive grant application, for two pieces of Zebra security work. The Zcash Foundation published the advisory crediting me as the sole reporter, and the Zebra 6.4.0 release notes thank me by name for reporting it. The second is my fix to Zebra’s IPv6 peer limit, which let one cheap server fill all of a node’s connection slots. The Zcash Foundation then built on my fix to patch the Medium severity GHSA-jhpp-8h75-7pv5 , where a banned peer could come straight back from another address on the same server. The Zebra 6.4.0 release notes credit my issue for both the IPv6 limit and the ban fix. events.excerpt: This is the fourth post in a series expanding on our governance stack. [Post 0: Overview] | Post 1: The Iris Oracle | Post 2: Multi-JAM Federation . Today: Layer 2 — decisions without parties. The infrastructure problem (Layer 0) and the identity problem (Layer 1) are hard engineering challenges. Layer 2 — how we actually make decisions — is a different kind of hard. It is not an engineering problem. It is a mechanism design problem, and the failure modes are political. Every democratic system ever built has failed in at least one of the same ways: Token-weighted voting — the wealthy decide. One token, one vote is plutocracy by definition. Simple majority — ignores intensity of preference. A 51% majority with mild opinions overrides a 49% minority whose lives depend on the outcome. Representative democracy — creates permanent political classes who optimise for re-election, not for constituents. Party systems — force multidimensional human preferences into one-dimensional ideological alignments. And in all of the above: the actor with the largest megaphone wins. The best-funded campaign, the most viral narrative, the most charismatic demagogue systematically outcompetes the actor who is simply correct.
